composition: Nominal composition (wt%): Al 12, Mn 20, C 1, Fe balance; this lies within the tested Fe–Mn–Al–C ranges of the study (Al 9–12, Mn 10–20–30, C 0.4–1 wt%, Fe bal.). Aluminium is the principal density-reducing element of the Fe–Mn–Al–C system (more than 20% density reduction can be achieved by alloying at least ~16 wt% Al), but Al is also a strong α-phase former with low solubility in α and a tendency to promote ordering and embrittlement; Mn and C are therefore added as austenite stabilizers to improve the microstructure and mechanical properties of the quaternary alloy.
conclusions: The 12Al-20Mn-1C hot-rolled sample (357 HV) is the as-received reference state of its composition within a study aimed at mapping the different austenite-decomposition reactions of Fe–Mn–Al–C lightweight steels as a function of composition and tempering temperature. Relative to the other tested grades it is one of the harder hot-rolled conditions; upon 800 °C tempering this composition gains hardness up to 404 HV (the largest increase among the four alloys compared in Table 5), which the paper attributes to the balancing of Mn-driven austenite stabilization by the Al–C driving force for κ-carbide formation, leading to full austenitic decomposition via cellular transformation coupled with spinodal decomposition. The study's overall conclusion is that the best-performing microstructure among all the conditions examined is that of 9Al-10Mn-1C tempered at 600 °C (fine γ+κ lamellae with narrow inter-lamellar spacing, 439 HV), not the hot-rolled 12Al-20Mn-1C state.
mechanisms: Aluminium is the dominant density-reducing element of Fe–Mn–Al–C steels, but because it is a strong α-phase former that embrittles ferritic microstructures, Mn and C are added as austenite stabilizers so that a metastable austenitic (fcc) matrix can be retained after processing; this composition design underlies the 12Al-20Mn-1C alloy.

The hot-rolled state is produced by a two-stage thermal path: solution/hot deformation at 1150 °C followed by water quenching, which retains the high-temperature γ/α/κ phase configuration in a non-equilibrium, supersaturated condition rather than the equilibrium microstructure implied by CALPHAD at room temperature.

The paper treats the hot-rolled condition at 1150 °C as non-equilibrium, so it uses phase-fraction diagrams only qualitatively; the thermodynamic gradient in austenite stability between the hot-rolling temperature (1150 °C) and the tempering temperatures (600 °C / 800 °C) is what provides the driving force for the subsequent austenite decomposition of Fe–Mn–Al–C alloys.

For the 12% Al / 20% Mn group the austenite stability gradient is reversed relative to the 9% Al alloys — austenite is less stable at 800 °C than at 1150 °C — which is the thermodynamic reason 12Al-20Mn-1C tends to transform during tempering and, at 800 °C, undergoes full decomposition by cellular transformation plus spinodal decomposition with dense cuboidal κ-carbides.

In this alloy family the hot-rolled condition is not an end state but the shared 'as-received' reference against which each tempering-induced hardening mechanism (discontinuous precipitation, precipitation transformation, cellular transformation, spinodal decomposition) is measured quantitatively.
microstructure: For the hot-rolled 12Al-20Mn-1C condition the paper reports no specific microstructural description: optical microscopy was performed on the hot-rolled state of all alloys, but no optical or SEM/EDS result is given specifically for the hot-rolled 12Al-20Mn-1C (the detailed SEM/EDS characterization of this composition in Figs. 5–8 and Table 7 refers to its 800 °C tempered state, not to the as-received state). The paper explicitly notes that the hot-rolled condition at 1150 °C is not an equilibrium state, so CALPHAD phase-fraction diagrams (Thermo-Calc, 0–1300 °C) were used only qualitatively. For this 12% Al / 20% Mn composition the f.c.c. (austenite) field lines are shifted toward higher temperatures, so austenite is thermodynamically less stable at 800 °C than at 1150 °C — a reversal relative to the 9% Al alloys. The hot-rolled state corresponds to the high-temperature (1150 °C) phase configuration retained by water quenching.
processing: Process genealogy: (1) melting and casting — the alloyed steel was produced in a 100 kW vacuum induction furnace under vacuum and cast into a 0.5 kg ingot; (2) mechanical/thermo-mechanical processing — the ingot was hot-rolled at 1150 °C down to 5 mm flat products; (3) cooling — hot-rolling was followed by water quenching, which yields the hot-rolled (as-received) reference condition. This condition was used unmodified for hardness and optical microscopy; tempering treatments at 600 °C and 800 °C for 30 min followed by water quenching were applied to sibling heat-treated samples, not to this hot-rolled state.
properties: Vickers macro-hardness: 357 HV, measured through the thickness with a 5 kg load and 5 indentations per sample on the hot-rolled (as-received) condition. No tensile strength, elongation or other mechanical, physical, chemical or service properties are reported for this sample. This value is the hot-rolled baseline of the 12Al-20Mn-1C composition in the study's comparison tables (e.g. Table 5, where it rises to 404 HV after 800 °C tempering). Characterization techniques applied to the sample/condition set include Vickers macro-hardness testing and optical microscopy; SEM (SE and BSE), EDS and CALPHAD calculations were used on the study's samples but not specifically reported for the hot-rolled 12Al-20Mn-1C state.
summary: The 12Al-20Mn-1C hot-rolled sample is a Fe–Mn–Al–C lightweight steel with nominal composition 12 wt% Al, 20 wt% Mn and 1 wt% C, Fe balance. It was produced by vacuum induction melting and casting into a 0.5 kg ingot, hot-rolled at 1150 °C to a 5 mm flat product and water-quenched, giving the "hot-rolled (as-received)" reference state of the study. Its through-thickness Vickers macro-hardness is 357 HV. In the paper this state is the baseline against which the austenite-decomposition reactions (discontinuous precipitation, precipitation transformation, cellular transformation and spinodal decomposition) produced by 600 °C and 800 °C tempering are compared.
unmapped: The hot-rolled condition (1150 °C + water quenching) is the shared 'as-received' reference state used for comparison in all of the study's hardness tables (Tables 2, 4, 5, 8 and 9).

For 12Al-20Mn-1C only the hot-rolled hardness (357 HV) is reported; the paper's microstructural and EDS characterization of this composition (Figs. 5(c), 7 and 8(c,d), Table 7) pertains to its tempered states (600 °C / 800 °C), not to the hot-rolled state, so those micrographs must not be attributed to this sample.
The 12Al-20Mn-1C composition falls within the tested Fe–Mn–Al–C ranges of Table 1 (Al 9–12, Mn 10–20–30, C 0.4–1 wt%, Fe bal.).

In the 12% Al alloy group the thermodynamic gradient for austenite stability between hot-rolling and tempering is reported as reversed relative to the 9% Al alloys (Fig. 12(c)), i.e. austenite is less stable at 800 °C than at 1150 °C for 12Al-20Mn-1C.
